card.intuition: A system that lets users find available time slots, reserve them, and prevents double-booking. Availability is modeled as a set of slots per provider per day, and reservations contend on that slot so only one user can claim it. When traffic spikes (event drops), optimistic or row-level locking keeps reservations consistent.
card.analogy: A clinic's book: each page is one day, each line is a doctor with time slots. Two receptionists cannot both scribble their name onto the same line because the first one to write locks that line; everyone else sees it taken.
card.time_complexity: Checking availability is O(slots) per provider/day; claiming a slot is an O(1) contended write plus lock.
card.space_complexity: Storage grows with providers × days × slots; hyper-scale events need pre-allocated slot rows to survive hot rows.
when_to_use: Reserving finite resources (appointments, seats, rooms, inventory) without overselling one slot
Multi-tenant calendars where many users contend for the same provider
Scheduling behind a reminder and notification pipeline
gotchas: A simple read-then-write check races on popular slots — you need atomic claim (lock or conditional update)
Overbooking for no-shows is a business decision, but must be modeled deliberately, not left to race conditions
Cancellation and waitlists need their own flows or you leak capacity

steps.annotation: Users browse a provider's calendar to see open time slots.
The API reads availability and, on booking, tries to claim the chosen slot atomically.
The slot is updated under a lock; only one user can successfully claim it.
Background workers send reminders, expire pending holds, and backfill waitlisted users.
The winning user gets a confirmation; losers see the slot as taken.
